# Homelab Documentation

## Overview

Every machine in this house has a page, and every page lives in one git repository of markdown runbooks. I started the habit after a Sunday evening when I could not remember why a service had been moved to a particular host, and I spent two hours reading old shell history instead of watching a film. That evening was the last time I lost a whole evening to a question the notes should have answered. The repository is plain text, so it version-controls cleanly and survives any tool I stop using. I write the runbooks the way I would want to read them at one in the morning, with the exact commands and the exact order. Nothing in the repository is a secret; passwords and keys stay in the password manager, and the runbooks only reference the entry by name. A runbook I cannot follow half-asleep is a runbook that does not exist, so I test them by actually running them. The repository has grown to about forty pages now, and the older pages are the ones I reread most, because they cover the systems that change least. I keep the pages short on purpose, one screen each where I can, and I split a page the moment it tries to describe two different jobs. The repository is the first thing I open when a host misbehaves and the last thing I write when a change is finished, and that order, notes first and notes last, is what keeps it honest. I do not use a wiki or a notes app, because a plain file in a git repository is the one format I am confident I will still be able to read in ten years, and it diffs properly when I want to see what changed. The repository is backed up with everything else, and the only thing it costs me is the discipline to write the page while the job is still fresh.

## Setup

The repository has three parts. The first is an address table for the home network on 172.16.10.0/24, which lists every fixed address, the host that holds it, and a one-line note on what it does. That table is the single place I look first when something on the network misbehaves, and it is the page most often opened on my phone. The second is a service inventory, one row per service, naming the host, the port, the data directory, and where the backup of that data lands. When I wonder whether a service has a copy, I read the inventory rather than opening three shells and hoping. The third part is the runbooks themselves.

Each runbook follows the same template, with a short description, a prerequisites section, the numbered steps, and a rollback section that says how to undo the work if it goes wrong. I keep the template itself in the repository so a new runbook starts from something consistent rather than from whatever I last wrote. The rollback section is the one I make myself fill in even when the job looks harmless, because a job that looks harmless is exactly the one I do without thinking. I commit each change with a plain message and push to a private remote, so the history of a change is available when I want to know when a machine gained a setting. I also keep a checked-out copy on the spare laptop. The address table doubles as a checklist, since a host with a row but no page is a host I have not documented yet, and reading the two side by side is how I spot the gap before it matters. Every runbook names the date I last ran it, so an old date is a hint that the page may no longer match the machine.

## Maintenance

Once a quarter I sit down and read the whole repository against reality. I open the address table and ping each host, I check that each row in the service inventory still points at a live service, and I click through the runbooks for the pieces I have changed since the last pass. Anything stale gets corrected on the spot rather than left for later, because the later version never comes. I also check that the template is still the one the newest runbooks use, since drift creeps into templates without anyone deciding it should. The review takes about ninety minutes and it is the single most valuable routine in the homelab. After the pass I tag the commit so I can see later which revision was last verified. Anything that turned out to be wrong during a real incident gets fixed that same evening, while I still remember the detail, because the memory of what actually happened is the most valuable thing I have and it fades by morning. I do the review in one sitting rather than in pieces, because a pass that is spread over a month is really no pass at all; by the time I reach the last page I have forgotten what I checked on the first. If the quarter slips I do not skip the pass, I move it a week and keep the count honest, and I would rather do a short pass than a perfect one that never happens. The pass is written down with a date at the top, so the next one has an obvious starting point.

## Notes

The value is not in the words, it is in the fact that the words match the machines. Documentation that has drifted is worse than none, because it sends me down the wrong path with confidence. I write runbooks only for jobs I expect to repeat, and I delete ones that describe a machine I no longer own, so the repository stays smaller than my ambition for it. The rollback section is the part I am proudest of, because it forces me to think about the failure before I cause it, and twice now it has stopped me making a change I had not thought through. I keep a copy of the repository checked out on the spare laptop as well, so a broken workstation does not lock me out of my own notes, and I keep a printed copy of the three most critical pages in a drawer for the same reason. The pages I regret most are the ones I wrote from memory a week after the fact, because a week is long enough to smooth over the exact step that gave me trouble. Writing while the shell is still warm is the habit that makes the whole repository worth keeping.
